statements.claim: Shamvara tells his charioteer: "take my car to the enemy soon. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong."
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.253 (Dutt): "filled with anger Shamvara said to his charioteer:—'O hero, do you soon take my car to the enemy. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong.'"

statements.claim: Pradyumna, son of Krishna and Rukmini, is the baby Shamvara had snatched away and meant to destroy, now grown to manhood.
statements.evidence: Passage 1.253: Shamvara laments "Why did I not kill him in his infancy?" while addressing him as "son of Rukshmini"; corpus chain (DKS_0318) covers his abduction and the slaying of Shamvara's four ministers.

statements.claim: Pradyumna had already cut down Shamvara's four chief ministers until the army fled from him.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain previous title (DKS_0318): "Pradyumna slays the four Danava ministers — Durdhara, Ketumali, Shatruhanta and Pramardana — one by one, and their army flees in terror."

statements.claim: Pradyumna's first golden shaft cut to Shamvara's vitals, and the demon reeled, clutched the reins and lost consciousness, recovering a few moments later.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "That arrow cutting to his very vitals, Shamvara... was greatly bewildered. And holding the reins of the car he lost consciousness. Regaining his consciousness a few moments after..."

statements.claim: Shamvara loosed seventy sharpened arrows; Pradyumna's seven shafts cut all seventy into seven parts before they reached him; then seventy winged arrows and a thousand more hid the sun.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "struck Krishna's son with seventy sharpened arrows. Pradyumna, with seven shafts, cut off those arrows into seven parts... And with seventy sharpened winged arrows he struck Shamvara... with a thousand beautiful winged arrows... the sky was so enshrouded by darkness that even the sun was not visible."

statements.claim: Shamvara dispelled the arrow-darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car, which Pradyumna sliced to pieces by light-handedness.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Seeing it Shamvara dispelled that darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car... Pradyumna too, displaying light-handedness, cut off those arrows into many pieces with his knotty shafts."

statements.claim: Shamvara's illusory trees were burned to ash by fiery weapons; his downpour of stones was swept away by airy weapons.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara, by his illusory powers, showered trees... destroyed them all by discharging fiery weapons. When all the trees were reduced to ashes Shamvara made a downpour of stones which Pradyumna removed from the battle-field by means of airy weapons."

statements.claim: Shamvara hurled illusory lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses and cloud-like elephants, which the Gandharva weapons cut to pieces.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "throwing on Pradyumna's car lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses and cloud-like elephants. Kāma however, with Gandharva weapons, cut them off into many pieces."

statements.claim: Shamvara raised illusory elephants with sixty heads each, ridden by expert drivers; Pradyumna's illusory lions destroyed them as the sun sends away the night.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "He showered youthful, well-decked elephants with sixty heads each... ridden by expert drivers... as the sun sends away the night so the illusory lions, created by the intelligent son of Rukshmini, destroyed the illusory elephants."

statements.claim: Pradyumna checked the Sunmohini Maya (the creation of the architect Maya) with his weapon of consciousness.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara... created Sunmohini Māyā... the creation of Maya, discharged by Shamvara, the powerful Pradyumna obstructed it with his Sanjnā (consciousness) weapon."

statements.claim: Pradyumna's eight-legged sharabhas pursued Shamvara's illusory lions as the wind scatters clouds.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Pradyumna took up Gandharva weapons and created Sharabhas... having eight legs, claws and teeth, pursued the lions. As the wind scatters clouds so those Sharabhas... pursued the lions."

statements.claim: Shamvara's inner doubt: "Alas! How stupid I am. Why did I not kill him in his infancy?... Only the dread illusion of serpents, taught to him by the great god Hara, remains."
statements.evidence: 1.253: Shamvara's thought quoted almost verbatim: "Alas! How stupid I am. Why did I not kill him in his infancy?... The dreadful illusion of serpents, which the great god Hara, the destroyer of Asuras, instructed me in, is only known to me."

statements.claim: Serpents full of burning venom fettered Pradyumna with his car, horses and charioteer; garudas appeared at his mere thought and destroyed them.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "Shamvara displayed that illusion of serpents full of burning venom, which fettered Pradyumna with his car, horses and charioteer... As soon as the high-souled Pradyumna thought of it Garudas began to move about and destroy the venomous serpents."

statements.claim: Gods and asuras cried "Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukmini, the illusion is dispelled by you, and we are pleased."
statements.evidence: 1.253: "the gods and Asuras, eulogising him said 'Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukshmini. On account of the illusion being dispelled by you we have been pleased.'"

statements.claim: Shamvara's remaining weapon was the golden club conferred by goddess Uma, able to dispel all illusion and kill all asuras, with which he had already sent many demons to Yama.
statements.evidence: 1.253: "the goddess Umā conferred that on me and said... this club which can dispell all forms of illusion and kill all the Asuras. I have with this club despatched to the abode of Yama..."

notes: All events, dialogue and weapon sequence match Harivamsha 1.253 nearly verbatim. Poetic flourishes ("rode it like a storm", "In the end it was the arrows that gave out first") are connective narration; the club-ending dovetails with the passage's closing lines.

statements.claim: Narada, sent by Indra, descended from the sky to Pradyumna on the battlefield — an ascetic with matted locks, a vina and a face bright as fire.
statements.evidence: Pack index: "Sent by Indra, Narada reminds Pradyumna of his former birth as Kama"; Harivamsha 1.257 describes Narada "covered entirely with matted locks and with the Vinā in his hand... effulgent like fire".

statements.claim: Pradyumna had been stolen as an infant by Shamvara, grown to youth in the demon's household, trained in arms, and now stood against his kidnapper.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.253: Shamvara reflects "Why did I not kill him in his infancy? Now this wicked-minded one has attained to youth and mastered all the weapons"; abduction and upbringing are the established corpus chain (DKS_0318-0319).

statements.claim: Narada revealed: "Remember your pristine birth, O hero. You are Kama... born again in the house of Krishna as Pradyumna."
statements.evidence: Evidence excerpt (Harivamsha 1.253): "Nārada... said to Pradyumna:—'...remember your pristine birth. O hero, you are Kāma...'"; Pradyumna's parentage (Krishna's son, raised in his house) is stated throughout 1.253.

statements.claim: Narada gave Pradyumna the Vaishnava weapons and a coat of mail.
statements.evidence: Pack index/summary: "gives him the Vaishnava weapons and a coat of mail, and bids him slay Shamvara and reclaim his wife Mayavati."

statements.claim: Narada's task: "Having killed Shamvara in the battlefield with the Vaishnava weapons, take your own wife Mayavati and go to Dwaraka."
statements.evidence: Evidence excerpt (Harivamsha 1.253): "having killed Shamvara in the battle-field with Vaishnava weapons take your own wife Māyāvati and go to Dwārakā."

statements.claim: The reason Shamvara's magic never held Pradyumna was that something in him was older than the demon's art — he was Kama born again.
statements.evidence: Packs confirm Pradyumna is Kama reborn (the 1.253 passage even calls him 'Kāma' in the Gandharva-weapons verse), but the causal reflection on why the illusions failed is the story's connective interpretation, not a stated source fact.

statements.claim: Pradyumna turned his chariot toward Shamvara's golden car as the demon reached for the golden club no god or demon could withstand.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.253: Shamvara thinks "I have a golden club resembling the rod of Death which even the gods and Asuras cannot withstand in the battle-field"; 1.253 ending and DKS_0319 close on him reaching for it.

notes: Identity revelation, weapons and mission all match the pack excerpt/index. Reflection paragraphs (childhood as apprenticeship, internal realization) are connective. Note the pack's cited chapter is 1.253 for all of 0319-0320; no factual discrepancies found.

statements.claim: A hurricane with lightning and thunder broke over Dwaraka; Narada, matted-locked and vina in hand, appeared, and the foul weather vanished the instant he touched the ground.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.257: "there blew a hurricane accompanied with the muttering of clouds charged with lighting... Nārada appeared there covered entirely with matted locks and with the Vinā in his hand... As soon as that foremost of ascetics, Nārada touched the ground the unfair weather disappeared."

statements.claim: Duryodhana had undertaken a sacrifice at Hastinapura, and all the kings travelling to it turned aside to see Krishna, drawn by his fame and Dwaraka's wonder.
statements.evidence: 1.257: "Duryodhana undertook the celebration of a sacrifice in Hastināpur and all the kings set out for (that city). Hearing of Janārddana with his sons... arrived at Krishna's palace."

statements.claim: The gathered kings were Duryodhana, the sons of Dhritarashtra, the sons of the Pandavas, Dhrishtadyumna, and the kings of Pandya, Chola, Kalinga, Vahlika, Dravida and Khasa with their armies.
statements.evidence: 1.257: "The king Duryodhana and others who were under the subjection of Dhritarashtra, the sons of Pandu, Dhristadyumna and others, the kings of Pandya, Chola, Kalinga, Vahlika Drāvida and Khasa with eighteen Akshowhinis of soldiers arrived."

statements.claim: Krishna welcomed the kings according to age and rank, seated them properly, and shone on his golden throne like the autumnal sun.
statements.evidence: 1.257: "showing them civilities according to their age and place Krishna sat on his golden throne. The kings too occupied seats according to their ranks... shone in the midst of those kings like the autumnal sun."

statements.claim: Narada hailed Krishna: "O thou of large arms, thou alone hast become an object of wonder to the gods... there is none blessed like thee in the world."
statements.evidence: 1.257: Narada's words quoted nearly verbatim in the story.

statements.claim: Krishna replied: "Yes, I am an object of surprise and good luck, especially in the matter of presents."
statements.evidence: 1.257: "Thus addressed the powerful Krishna, smilingly said:—'Yes I am an object of surprise and good luck, especially in the matter of presents.'"

statements.claim: The puzzled kings asked the meaning, and Krishna bade the twice-born Narada relate it; Narada sat on a white golden seat and explained.
statements.evidence: 1.257: kings "could not make out the mystery... 'If we are worthy of listening to the true import we wish to hear it'... 'the twice-born Nārada will relate it'... 'Nārada, seated on a white golden seat... began to explain those words.'"

statements.claim: On the Ganga bank Narada met a mountain-huge, four-legged tortoise with two coatings, soaked, moss-covered, its skin hard as an elephant's, which declared Ganga more blessed than itself.
statements.evidence: 1.257: "I saw a tortoise... huge like a mountain, had four legs, two coatings, was soaked with water, and covered with mosses. Its skin was hard like that of an elephant... 'What wonder is there in me, O Muni? And how can I be blessed? This Gangā... is blessed in whom range hundreds and thousands of animals like myself.'"

statements.claim: Each praised being pointed onward: Ganga to the ocean, ocean to the earth, earth to the mountains, mountains to Brahma, Brahma to the Vedas, the Vedas to the sacrifices, until the chain ended in Vishnu — and great is a sacrifice accompanied by presents.
statements.evidence: Pack summary: "Narada recounts a journey from tortoise to Ganga, ocean, earth, mountains, Brahma, the Vedas and the Yajnas, each deferring to the next, until the riddle resolves in Vishnu with dakshina"; excerpt (1.257): "Vishnu alone is the great wonder... great is a Yajna accompanied with presents."

statements.claim: The riddle's answer: Krishna's "presents" reply was true because the blessed one is he whom all the giving of the world finally reaches.
statements.evidence: The chain ending in Vishnu-with-dakshina is supported; the sentence decoding Krishna's pun as 'the end of all giving' is the narrator's interpretive gloss, consistent with but not verbatim in the pack.

notes: Court scene, dialogue, tortoise encounter and deference chain all map to Harivamsha 1.257. The closing line about the storm not daring to return is atmosphere. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Krishna mounted Garuda amid conch shells, bugles, bards and victory-blessings; with Balarama and Pradyumna on the bird's back they flew toward Sonitpura to bring down Bana.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.264: "with the sound of conch-shells and bugles, the songs of bards and panegyrists by thousands and blessings of men exclaiming victory Janarddana appeared..."; "Desirous of killing Vāna the lotus-eyed Keshava assumed a form having eight arms and resembling a mountain."

statements.claim: Krishna took an eight-armed, mountain-like form with innumerable heads: right hands holding sword, discus, club and arrows; left hands the leathern guard, Shranga bow, thunderbolt and conch.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Janārddana, the holder of Shranga-bow, assumed innumerable heads. In his four right hands he had sword, discus, club and arrows and by his left four hands he held the leathern protector, the Srānga-bow, the thunder-bolt and conch-shell."

statements.claim: Balarama (Sankarshana) rode with a thousand forms and white weapons, shining like the rising moon above Kailasha; Pradyumna was radiant as Sanatkumara.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Sanghkarshana, holding a thousand forms and white weapons... like the mount Kailāsha with its summit, shone like the rising moon"; "the high-souled Pradyumna assumed a form like that of Sanatkumār."

statements.claim: Garuda's wings shook mountains and obstructed the wind as he crossed the sacred route of the Siddhas and Charanas.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "shaking innumerable mountains and obstructing the course of the wind with the forcible flapping of his wings the powerful Vinatā's son went on. Endued with the speed of the mind he crossed the most sacred route of the Siddhas and Chāranas."

statements.claim: Balarama noticed their sudden golden hue and asked if they had come beside Mount Sumeru; Krishna explained that the blazing fire stationed in Bana's city had possessed them with the effulgence of the fire of oblation.
statements.evidence: 1.264: Rāma: "we have all on a sudden been shorn of our effulgence? We have all a golden hue... Have we come to the side of the mount Sumeru?" Krishna: "To protect him, the fire, stationed in his city, is coming out blazing... we have been possessed by the effulgence of the fire of oblation: this has changed our colour."

statements.claim: Garuda, told to find a means, assumed a thousand mouths, drank profuse water from the etherial Ganga in the sky, and showered it on the blazing fire, extinguishing it at once.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Garuda, capable of assuming forms at will, assumed a thousand mouths... went to the etherial Gangā. Then drinking profuse water, he began to shower it on the fire... the fire was at once extinguished."

statements.claim: Garuda marveled: "Oh! How powerful is this fire... like the fire at the end of a cycle. It disfigured the color of even the intelligent Krishna."
statements.evidence: 1.264: Suparna: "Oh! How powerful is this fire like that at the end of a cycle. It disfigured the color of even the intelligent Krishna."

statements.claim: The fires, followers of Rudra, saw three dreadful men of many forms riding Garuda and wondered who they were and why they had come.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Seeing them the fires, the followers of Rudra, thought:—'Who are these three dreadful men of many forms who are riding Garuda? Why have they come here?'" (pack ends the story scene before they attack; the attack is DKS_0323).

notes: Full flight, golden-hue dialogue and fire-quenching sequence match Harivamsha 1.264. Minor nuance: in the source it is Garuda's beauty that "increased by Hari's energy became immense" — the story attaches the phrase loosely to the ascent scene; treated as connective narration, not a contradiction. Story ends before the fire-gods' attack, faithful to the pack's cut.

statements.claim: The fire-gods, followers of Rudra, rose around Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna on Garuda, asked who the three dreadful men were, and, unable to settle it, attacked them.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.264: "Seeing them the fires, the followers of Rudra, thought... could not settle anything. They then began to fight with the three Yadus. A great noise arose when they engaged in fighting."

statements.claim: Garuda flew on with the speed of thought, crossing the sacred route of the Siddhas and Charanas, and the fire-gods met the travellers before Bana's city came into view.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Endued with the speed of the mind he crossed the most sacred route of the Siddhas and Chāranas"; the fire-gods' fight occurs en route, since Narada only sights Vana's city afterwards ("Thereupon seeing Vāna's city from a distance...").

statements.claim: Krishna fought in his eight-armed mountain form with sword, discus, club, arrows, the great bow, the thunderbolt and the conch.
statements.evidence: 1.264: eight arms holding sword, discus, club, arrows, leathern protector, Shranga-bow, thunderbolt and conch-shell.

statements.claim: Bana heard the uproar and despatched a messenger fleet as the mind; Angira, chief of the fires, also sent a man to hurry to the battle.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "the intelligent Chief of the Fires Angirā sent a man to the scene of the action... 'Soon proceed where the battle is raging.' Another Asura, fleet like the mind, was quickly despatched by Vanā saying 'Go and see what is the matter.'"

statements.claim: The messenger found the five principal fire-gods Kalmasha, Kusuma, Dahana, Shoshana and Tapana fighting with their armies, the five Swadha-gods Pithara, Pataga, Swarna, Agadha and Vraja, and the two fire-gods in charge of Jyotisthoma and Vasatkara.
statements.evidence: 1.264 lists exactly these names: "Kalmāsha, Kusuma, Dahana, Shoshana and the highly powerful Tapana... Pithara, Pataga, Swarna, Agādha and Vraja, these five presiding gods of Swadhā... the two highly effulgent fire-gods, in charge of Jyotisthoma and Vasatkāra."

statements.claim: The great sage Angira led them on a fiery car, mace uplifted, shining over the battlefield.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Ascending a fiery car the great saint Angirā, uplifting his effulgent mace, was shining in that battle-field, in the midst of fire-gods."

statements.claim: Krishna smiled again and again and told the fire-gods to wait patiently — their destruction was near and they would fly away on all sides.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Krishna... smiled again and again and said:—'O ye fire-gods, wait patiently a few moments. The time of your destruction is drawing near. Within a moment, consumed by the energy of my weapons, you shall have to fly away on all sides.'"

statements.claim: Angira charged Krishna with a burning trident; Krishna sheared off his mace with crescent-headed arrows and struck him on the breast with a death-like arrow, and Angira fell bathed in blood.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "as if to take Krishna's life Angirā ran with a burning Trishula in his hand. Then cutting off his mace with crescent-shaped and sharpened arrows... struck Angirā on the breast with a death-like-arrow. Thereat Angirā fell down bathed in blood and with his body mangled."

statements.claim: The four fire-gods who are sons of Brahma fled with the whole host back to Bana's city.
statements.evidence: 1.264: "Seeing it the four fire-gods, the sons of Brahmā along with others speedily fled away to Vāna's city."

notes: Battle narrative, named fire-gods and Krishna's dialogue track Harivamsha 1.264 closely. Opening recap of the fire-quenching and the 'second sun' simile are connective. No unsupported or contradicted facts.

statements.claim: Chitralekha came to Dwaraka, settled near the palace of Vasudeva, and while thinking saw the ascetic Narada meditating in the water; she saluted him with bowed head.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.266: "Having arrived at the city of Dwārakā and living near the palace of Vāsudeva Chitrālekha began to think... she saw the ascetic Nārada engaged in meditation in the water... Having saluted him she stood before him hanging her head down."

statements.claim: Chitralekha told Narada she had come as a messenger to take Aniruddha: Bana of Sonitpura had a beautiful daughter Usha, who had selected Aniruddha as husband by a goddess's boon, having never met him except in a dream.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "I have come here as a messenger for taking Aniruddha with me... A great Asura, by name Vāna, lives in the city of Shonitapura. He has a most beautiful daughter by name Ushā... he has been selected by her as her husband on account of the boon given by the goddess." Dream-marriage is confirmed in her later speech to Aniruddha ("whom you saw in a dream and married").

statements.claim: Chitralekha feared Krishna's wrath: Bana was too powerful for Aniruddha to defeat, but the large-armed Krishna would vanquish the thousand-armed asura; when angered Krishna could consume even the three worlds.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "Highly powerful is the great Asura Vāna in battle, so Aniruddha will not be able to defeat him. The large-armed Keshava will vanquish that thousand-armed Asura... When angered the large armed Keshava can consume even the three worlds."

statements.claim: Narada offered protection and gave her the Tamasika learning: "Accept the Tamasika learning... that can infatuate all the worlds," saying he was fond of seeing battles.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "I offer you protection... if any encounter takes place when you steal away Aniruddha to the appartment of maidens remember me... I am much fond of seeing battles... Accept the Tāmasa learning which can infatuate all the worlds and which I have mastered by practising hard austerities."

statements.claim: In the centre of Dwaraka Chitralekha found the palace of Kama, and beside it Aniruddha's palace with golden altars, gold-and-sapphire pillars, garlands, water jars, peacocks on the turrets and celestial buildings filled with Gandharva music.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "going to the centre of Dwaravati she saw the beautiful palace of Kāma. Near it she saw Airuddha's palace. It had golden altars and pillars made of gold and sapphires... beautiful figures of peacocks on the turret... filled with the music of the Gandharvas."

statements.claim: Aniruddha sat like Kubera drinking Madhvika wine amid hundreds of beautiful women, yet showed dislike even for drinking; Chitralekha concluded his mind was busy with the dream.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "Kāma's son playing in the midst of highly beautiful women as the moon shines amongst the stars... Seated like Kuvera... Aniruddha was drinking Mādhvika wine... he was showing dislike even for drinking. Thereupon thinking 'Surely his mind is busy with the dream,' Chitralekhhā was shorn of anxiety."

statements.claim: Hiding in the sky above the palace, Chitralekha told Aniruddha she had been sent by Usha, whom he saw in a dream and married and who cherished him at heart — weeping, yawning and sighing; she would live if he went to her, and die in his absence.
statements.evidence: 1.266: "I have been sent to you by Ushā whom you saw in a dream and married and who has been cherishing you at her heart... that maiden is again and again weeping, yawning and sighing for seeing you... she will live if you go there. Forsooth, in your absence she will die."

statements.claim: By her Tamasika illusion Chitralekha overpowered everyone in the palace except the prince, and carried Aniruddha through the sky to Usha's rooms in Sonitpura.
statements.evidence: 1.266: Chitralekha resolves "By my Tamasik illusion I will overpower all except Aniruddha"; the chapter title is "Chitralekha Unites Aniruddha with Usha," and the pack's truncated passage opens that very delivery.

notes: Dialogue and detail track Harivamsha 1.266 closely (Narada's protection speech is near-verbatim). The final claim about the abduction to 'a maiden's rooms where Usha was waiting' is the chapter's stated outcome. No issues.

statements.claim: Recap: Usha chose Aniruddha in a dream by a goddess's boon; her friend Chitralekha obtained Narada's blessing and Tamasika learning in Dwaraka, spoke to Aniruddha of Usha's weeping and pining, and carried him through the sky to Sonitpura.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.266 (same chapter as this story's citation): Usha's boon-chosen dream husband, Narada's Tāmasa learning, the message of weeping/yawning/sighing and 'she will live if you go there' are all in the passage; chapter title confirms the uniting with Usha.

statements.claim: Word reached Bana that his daughter was living with the Yadava prince Pradyumna's son, and he sent his soldiers, the Daityas and Danavas, to kill the intruder.
statements.evidence: Evidence excerpt (1.266): "taking up a dreadful Parigha... he killed the Daityas... Having driven with Parigha the Dānavas from the battle-field..." — the host he fought were the Daityas and Danavas, implying Bana sent his soldiers against him; index summary: "When Vana discovers Usha living with Aniruddha and sends his soldiers to kill him."

statements.claim: Aniruddha seized a dreadful parigha (great iron club), killed the Daityas who pressed closest, and single-handedly drove the whole Danava host from the field.
statements.evidence: Evidence excerpt (1.266): "taking up a dreadful Parigha... he killed the Daityas... Having driven with Parigha the Dānavas from the battle-field the highly powerful hero Aniruddha delightfully set up a leonine shout."

statements.claim: After the field was empty Aniruddha raised a leonine shout of delight that rang across Sonitpura.
statements.evidence: Evidence excerpt (1.266): "the highly powerful hero Aniruddha delightfully set up a leonine shout."

statements.claim: Bana understood what his soldiers could not do, and before long the Yadava prince would find himself a prisoner in the city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.267 (next story's pack): "the heroic Aniruddha was imprisoned in the city of Shonita along with Ushā by Bali's son king Vāna" — the imprisonment follows directly from the rout; teaser consistent with the corpus chain.

statements.claim: Chitralekha had stolen the sleeping prince out of his own palace.
statements.evidence: The pack does not describe Aniruddha's state at the moment of abduction (passage truncated before the carrying-away); 'sleeping' is a small connective detail, and the claim that she stole/carried him away from his palace is supported by 1.266.

notes: Parigha fight, Daitya/Danava rout and leonine shout match the 1.266 excerpt. 'The sleeping prince' is the only detail beyond the pack and is trivial connective narration. Recap paragraphs accurately compress DKS_0324.

statements.claim: Aniruddha was imprisoned in Bana's city of Sonitpura along with Usha by Bana, Bali's son.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.267: "While the heroic Aniruddha was imprisoned in the city of Shonita along with Ushā by Bali's son king Vāna."

statements.claim: Aniruddha was held by a strong noose of serpents, and his strength and club were useless to him.
statements.evidence: 1.267: the goddess "with her fingers cut off the strong noose of serpents"; imprisonment in chains is the premise of the hymn. The club detail is a fair inference from his disarmament, presented as connective framing.

statements.claim: Seeking refuge with the goddess Kaumari for his own safety, Aniruddha sang a hymn saluting the eternal prime deity Lord Narayana and chanting the glories of Chandi, the goddess Katyayani, worshipped by gods, rishis and rakshasas, reciting the names sung by Hari.
statements.evidence: 1.267: "he, seeking refuge with goddess Koumāri for his own safety, sang a hymn in her praise. Having saluted the endless, undecaying, eternal prime deity the Lord Narayana, I chant the glories of Chandi, the worshipful goddess Katyāyani... adored by the gods, Rishis and Rakshasas, reciting the names sung by Hari."

statements.claim: In the hymn Aniruddha bowed to the sister of Indra and Vishnu, who confers honours, and asked: "Release me from my bonds, and give me life and health."
statements.evidence: 1.267: "For my well being I bow unto the sister of Mahendra and Vishnu. Being cleansed and with my mind purified... I bow unto thee who dost confer honors, do thou release me from my bonds and give me life and health."

statements.claim: Durga, fond of her votaries, appeared where Aniruddha lay in chains, consoled him, and with her own fingers cut the strong noose of serpents.
statements.evidence: 1.267: "the great goddess Durgā went where Aniruddha was kept in chains. The goddess, fond of her votaries, released Aniruddha... consoled him. The powerful hero then saluted her. Thereupon the goddess with her fingers cut off the strong noose of serpents."

statements.claim: The goddess promised: "O Aniruddha, wait here for a few days more. The holder of the discus, the slayer of the Daityas, will cut off the thousand arms of Vana, release you from your fetters, and take you to his own city."
statements.evidence: 1.267: Durga's words quoted nearly verbatim in the story ("will cut off the thousand arms of Vāna, release you from your fetters and take you to his own city").

statements.claim: Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna were already flying toward Sonitpura on Garuda to make the goddess's words good.
statements.evidence: Corpus chain next title: "Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna Fly to Sonitpura on Garuda" (Harivamsha 1.264 flight sequence); consistent with the goddess's promise of rescue by the discus-holder.

statements.claim: Bana seized Aniruddha and threw him into chains, together with Usha who would not be parted from him, answering the leonine shout.
statements.evidence: The pack states the resulting state (imprisoned together by Bana) but the passage describing the actual capture is not in the pack; the attribution to Bana and Usha's refusal to part are connective bridging consistent with 1.267's opening.

notes: Hymn content, Katyayani/Durga epiphany, finger-cutting of the serpent noose and the goddess's promise all match Harivamsha 1.267 near-verbatim. Capture mechanics are connective bridging; no contradictions.
